name: Antonio Vivaldi
why: His first wave, from 1926 to 1933, came mostly in modern orchestral arrangements led by Toscanini, Mengelberg and Bernardino Molinari. The return was led by Guido Cantelli, with 21 of the 42 performances from 1953-54 to 1959-60, and then Leonard Bernstein. It came during the postwar Vivaldi revival.
story: Vivaldi’s comeback rode on a young conductor Toscanini called the most gifted he had met in his long career. Guido Cantelli brought the concertos back to the Philharmonic in 1954, in the middle of the postwar Vivaldi boom. Two years later he was killed in a plane crash at Orly, a week after La Scala named him music director.

name: William Walton
why: Before the gap, John Barbirolli, then the music director, led 11 of his 18 performances, mostly Façade. Walton faded after Barbirolli left. He came back when he conducted his own music at Lewisohn Stadium in August 1963; Josef Krips, Malcolm Sargent and André Kostelanetz kept him on the chart for the next few seasons.
story: “I seriously advise all sensitive composers to die at the age of 37,” Walton said. His first New York run belonged to John Barbirolli, who premiered his second Façade suite with the Philharmonic in 1938. When Barbirolli went home, Walton faded, until he came back to conduct his own music at Lewisohn Stadium in August 1963.

name: György Ligeti
why: Before the gap, Pierre Boulez’s Lontano in the 1970s (Boulez led 9 of 21 performances). The return began in the 2006-07 season, months after Ligeti died in June 2006, with Alan Gilbert leading the Violin Concerto. Gilbert later conducted Le Grand Macabre (2010), and Esa-Pekka Salonen brought three works in 2010-11.
story: Most people first heard Ligeti in 2001: A Space Odyssey, where Kubrick used his music “without Ligeti’s knowledge”; Ligeti sued, and they settled out of court. He died in June 2006, and the Philharmonic’s return to him began that autumn. In 2013 Alan Gilbert put him back beside Kubrick, in a concert built around 2001.

name: Richard Rodgers
why: A Lewisohn Stadium regular: his show tunes were played there every summer from 1945 to 1964, and he dropped out when the Stadium summers ended. He came back through a new format, Broadway nights in the main season: Barbara Cook singing Rodgers in 2007, then a staged concert of Carousel in 2013.
story: Rodgers didn’t go out of fashion; his venue did. His songs were a summer fixture at Lewisohn Stadium from 1945 to 1964, and when the Philharmonic stopped playing there he vanished from its programs. He came back in 2007 with Barbara Cook’s 80th-birthday concerts, and in 2013 with a staged Carousel.

name: Carl Nielsen
why: One conductor’s project. Alan Gilbert led every Nielsen performance from 2010-11 to 2014-15 while recording all the symphonies and concertos for Dacapo, Denmark’s national label, ahead of Nielsen’s 150th birthday in 2015.
story: The Philharmonic made Nielsen famous, then forgot him. Bernstein’s 1962 recording of the Fifth Symphony was his international breakthrough; then the orchestra dropped him for 25 years, until Alan Gilbert, who came to Nielsen in Sweden, “where Danish music is totally standard fare,” recorded all the symphonies and concertos with it.
